3. Anyway, the object of the Ordinance of 1959 is to provide for better control of manufacture and sale of food for human consumption. Section 3(1) of the Ordinance of 1959 enumerates the conditions/ circumstances under which an article of food shall be deemed to be adulterated. Amonst others, Clause (e) of Sub-section (1) of Section 3 deems an article of food to be adulterated if it does not comply with any standered provided by or under this Ordinance or any other law for the time being in force and Clause (t) thereof provides that if an article of food contains or is mixed or diluted with any substance in such quantity as is to the prejudice of the purchaser or consumer or in such proportion as diminishes in any manner the food value or nutritive qualities which it possessed in its pure, normal, underteriorated and sound condition, it shall be deemed to be adulterated. Section 5 of the Ordinance of 1959 provides that the Government may determine by rules-(a) the normal constituents and the values of the chemical and physical constants of any article of food: and (b) in respect of a sample of any article of food, the deficiency in any such constituent or the addition of any extraneous matter or the proportion of water which shall, for the purpose of this Ordinance and until the contrary is proved, raise a presumption that such article is adulterated. As per Section 49 of the Ordinance of 1959, the Government may, subject to the condition of previous publication, make rules providing for, amogst others, the normal contituents and the values of the chemical and physical constants of any article of food and the definicies in, or addition to, any article of food which are to raise the presumption that such article is adulterated, and the conditions to be fulfilled in the case of mustard or rape seed oil. Section 12 of the Ordinance of 1959 provides that in the case of mustard or any other rape seed oil, the article manufactured or sold, as the case may be, shall be derived exclusively form mustard or any other rape seed, the case may be, and shall fulfill such other conditions as may be prescribed. The rules of 1967 were framed pursuant to Section 49 of the Ordinance of 1959. Rule 6 of the Rules of 1967 contemplates that any of the articles of food elaborated in the Schedul not confirming to the specification or specifications mentioned there under shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of Sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the Ordinance of 1959. Serial No.25 of the Schedule of the Rules of 1967 deals with mustered oil. According to Serial No. 25(d) of the Schedule, Free Fatty Acid (FFA) as oleic acid shall not be more than 1.25%. 

 19. As per the preamble of the Ordinance of 1959, its object is to provide for better control of manufacture and sale of food for human consumption. Sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the said Ordinance specifies the conditions/circumstances under which an article of food shall be deemed to be "adulterated". Clause (e) of Sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the Ordinance provides that an article of food shall be deemed to be "adultrated" if it does not comply with any standard provided by or under this Ordinance or any other law for the time being in force. Beside, Clause (0 of Sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the Ordinance of 1959 contemplates that an article of food shall be deemed to be "adulterated" if it contains or is mixed or diluted with any substance in such quantity as is to the prejudice of the purchaser or consumer or in such proportion as diminishes in any manner the food value or nutritive qualities which it possesses in its pure, normal, undeteriorated and sound condition. Section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance of 1959 enjoins that the Government may determine by rules the normal constituents and the values of the chemical and physical constants of any article of food. By dint of Section 49 Of the Ordinance of 1959, the Rules of 1967 were framed providing for, amongst others, the normal constituents and the values of the chemical and physical constants of any article of food referred to in Clause (a) of Sub-section (1) of Section 5 and the deficiencies in, or additions to, any article of food which are to raise the presumption that such article is adulterated referred to in Clause (b) of that Sub-section.
